205.t: When jazz was popular and its decline around 1960
205.s: Jazz faded from the 1950s as rock and roll took over; early rock sidemen still swung and Connie Kay played R&B.
205.ch: Careers, business and the music scene
205.q: Probably from the time I was born to — it seems like it started petering out in the 50s, somewhere in the 50s, we had to scuffle around. Of course there was a lot of bars that you could play, you know, cocktail lounges and all that, you could play some pretty nice, easy, light jazz. But it started…

205.t: The 1950s, rock and roll and discovering bebop
205.s: Rock and roll pushed big band and jazz aside, while he loved bebop and heard Parker and Miles.
205.q: Yeah, they did — yeah, they did. I never had any problem, before I went into the Army and after I was in the Army, I didn’t have too much problem getting work. But the Bill Haley and the Comets, and all that rock & roll really got into it as far as popularity was concerned I think. Real good music,…

337.t: The Metropole and the twist ending jazz there
337.s: At the Metropole he shared the stand with Tony Farrante's trio until go-go girls and rock took over; he closed it with Napoleon's trio and Krupa's quartet.
337.q: Yeah. I’ll explain that as shortly as I can. 195— around the Benny Goodman time or something like that, or maybe just before that because that’s how the word of mouth came for me to go with Benny, around 1955 I was playing at the Metropole when all the old time swingers were winding down, like…

337.t: Musicians forced to adapt to rock and dance crazes
337.s: Club date musicians had to adopt rock and go-go; it hurt many and he struggled after leaving Krupa.
337.q: Yeah everybody had to change. Everybody had to make a change. And you started, well club dates at that time were mostly swing or tunes, good tunes and so on like that. But when the twist came out, then everybody, from Peter Duchin on, from all the big bands, from Lester Lanin, they all had to…

104.t: Rock taking over while avant-garde jazz alienated listeners
104.s: They discuss how rock, the Beatles and studios chasing teenagers pushed jazz aside, while Miles and the avant-garde were said to be alienating audiences.
104.q: No, I remember that being said, either in print or by people, that . . . People like Miles. I think he was specifically mentioned, because they were alienating the audience. They didn’t seem to care if the audience listened. Just what you said. They were playing music that nobody understood. You’d…

104.t: Rock, fusion and smooth jazz changing the jazz scene
104.s: She recalls rock like Bill Haley and Chubby Checker casting a cloud over jazz, and they discuss Bitches Brew, Weather Report and the smooth saxophone sound.
104.q: I’m not sure when that happened, because I . . . for a minute I thought you were going back to that period when suddenly it seemed like rock took over.

124.t: The Apollo house band and rock and roll acts
124.s: The Apollo's house band could not play the new rock-and-roll groups, so Schiffman used a small house band and let acts bring their own musicians.
124.q: was so pitiful about, these fellas had the band in the Apollo, they didn't keep up with what was going on. What was really happening, you know. This is -- now you got -- come out of the rock and roll and the what? Rhythm and blues into the rock and roll, right? Now '40's, 50's and the 52 -- you…

124.t: Alan Freed and rock and roll displace big-band jazz
124.s: McRae says Freed's rock and roll made it hard for jazz records, and he recalls Stanley Turrentine recording "Broadway".
124.q: This will give you an idea what really happened to big bands. When Alan Freed came in -- this was the killing of a lot of things -- a lot of styles and things.

178.t: Changing styles: rock and roll, bossa nova and beat
178.s: They discuss having to play Dixieland, rock, bossa nova and the new beat, and agree the records are played behind the beat.
178.q: Not so much progressive. Bossanova. Oh yeah, Bossanova and Rumba, Sambos, Congo and all that kind of stuff too. But as far as I mean you have to play rock and roll, what do they call it again? Well they've got the twist for a while.

871.t: Melody Inn combo and rock and roll
871.s: He recalls his combo at the Melody Inn, a rock and roll drummer sitting in, his dislike of rock and roll, and the old cymbal pedal.
871.q: Now when I was working down here at the Melody Inn. We had a little combo down there. Saxophone player that played with me down there. Sunday. Harold Dajon. Harold Dajon was on sax. Same piano player was there with me playing. Simon Fraser.

623.t: Dixieland crowds, Alan Freed and the rise of rock
623.s: Crowds were large before rock; Alan Freed's Moondog episode and Dixieland's decline.
623.ch: Early life and New York years
623.q: Oh, a good-sized crowd. Yeah, lots of fans in those days. The so-called Dixieland was quite a big thing. This is pre-Elvis Presley. Pre-rock. In fact, I was living and working in New York when Alan Freed came out of, I think it was Cleveland, to break it up in New York and he came into town using…

261.t: Rock and roll question on second tape
261.s: Russell asks about rock and roll and Fats Domino's popularity.
261.q: I was going to ask what I think of it, since you were mostly associated with Pat Stomino, not that he's a real old-time musician and all that, and one of the old pioneers of the Dixie thing, but I wondered about your reactions to the rock and roll. What made him so sensational? Did you ever figure…

83.t: Effect of rock and roll on business; round-the-clock sessions and mixers
83.s: R&B got the outside attention but early rock brought the most work; Matassa worked days without going home and let trusted people such as Seth David mix sessions.
83.ch: Running the studio in the rock and roll boom
83.q: You know. The rhythm and blues things. The first. You know. Stuff. Was probably the most important. Because that's the stuff. They got. Outside attention.

272.t: Later posters: pickup dances, Slidell and rock-and-roll era billing
272.s: The interviewer reads later flyers, including a Slidell club billing him as father of jazz, and Pass Christian dates.
272.ch: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
272.q: We have skipped a clutter area there. Yeah. These are late things, huh? Yeah. He skipped quite a while during the compression when he was playing at Morrison's interview. Oh, yeah.

846.t: Small bands today, the Condon chapter and rock and roll
846.s: Young bands now play the old style; Souchon urges recording the old Negro musicians, who are not being succeeded, and criticises rock and roll.
846.q: Not only the, uh... Union bands, both Negro and white, but there's any number of young bands that are coming up. And that's one of the things...

715.t: Rock and roll and Dixieland demand
715.s: Allen says his band plays rock and roll when paid, and notes demand for Dixieland; the transcript degrades into a loop.
715.q: We mix stuff down like what we was. We played a little everything. We got to play rock and roll and catch ourselves along with some.

301.t: Moving to Opelousas and the music scene there
301.s: He took a job at the St. Andrew Club in 1943, married, and brought his wife back home; rock and roll has displaced older music.
301.q: Opelousas. Well, we opened a job there at the St. Andrew Club. I was in 43. I got married a couple years after. So I'm not glad to move there. Yeah. The wife didn't want to leave there. I did take her out on a couple of trips. And I know she wasn't satisfied and she started losing weight. So I say…

392.t: Rock, rhythm and blues and Smiling Joe
392.s: Rock fading, rhythm and blues returning, and Joe Robichaux's talent.
392.q: Well, it's on its way out now. I understand the biggest discotheque in, uh, New York called Arthur. They're for sale. And these things are dying on the street. There aren't too many of them left anyway, thank God, because with that, uh, amplification was too much. Too much. I mean, they weren't…

1054.t: Rock and roll versus jazz as party music in college
1054.s: Rock and roll rose as party music in college, but jazz suits mixed-age crowds while rock suits young rowdy parties.
1054.ch: Jazz as art form or party music
1054.q: Well, I think Rock and Roll was coming to the fore as party music. And I think it is now. Because it's earthier. Because it's earthier.

978.t: Dixieland, rock and roll and boogie woogie today
978.s: They discuss the style the current band plays, requests for old tunes at holiday dances, boogie woogie versus rock and roll, and why Dixieland lasts.
978.q: Now there's some people here in New Iberia, they are high and they want Dixon. Uh huh. That's when you play anything else, they want to ask you to stop. What style does Mr. Wilson's band, what style do you play in? Well we try to satisfy the people, try to give them some of the present day stuff.

1055.t: Friends turn from Dixieland to rock and roll
1055.s: He prefers more progressive music, while many friends switched to rock and roll after about 1953, though they have not wholly abandoned Dixieland.
1055.q: Well, I myself liked Dixieland well enough. I thought I'd progress some progressive music more. And a lot of my friends have switched to liking what they call rock and roll them.

311.s: He stuck to Lunceford, Goodman and Ellington styles and played only a couple of Beatles tunes.
311.q: Oh I played a couple of them, you know, a couple, to satisfy people. But that wasn’t my forte. I was more like Jimmie Lunceford, [inaudible] and other stuff you know and Benny Goodman stuff and Duke Ellington stuff, in that vein. Yeah.

667.t: Rock 'n' roll, the Beatles and the album 'Changes'
667.s: Rock did not hurt their club work, but their manager wanted current songs, leading to 'Changes' and 'Grass'.
667.ch: Rock era, electric piano, move east
667.q: Except in one respect and that was recording. Because at that time we had a manager, what was his name — Monty Kaye was our manager. And Monty Kaye wanted us to incorporate some current music, like Beatles and stuff. Our daughters loved the Beatles and they listened to it, and when we first heard…

317.t: Rock and roll, Canada and country and western
317.s: Jeannie turned professional in 1950; rock and roll hurt work so they played Toronto and Quebec, where they saw Dizzy, until country and western took over.

395.t: Cui Jian, Chinese rock, folk songs, and the Flower Drum Song
395.s: Rowe asks about young Chinese music; Jang recalls performing with rock icon Cui Jian, Tiananmen, and the preservation of folk songs.
395.q: Well I think perhaps what you’re suggesting is that there is maybe another transformation with the younger generation? I performed with Cui Jian who is the rock icon of China — China’s first rock icon I should say. As a result I had nothing but my name. He expressed © Hamilton College Jazz Archive…

119.t: Rock and roll, Elvis and country music
119.s: He did not care for Elvis, but remembers Grandpa Jones on the Grand Ole Opry and later came to see country as a cousin to jazz.
119.q: Yeah, I didn’t like Elvis. No. I says he’s a musician, I’m a musician, I says, his music doesn’t sound as good as mine. But he had that gyration going. Those knees going. So it’s show biz, you know, playing guitar. I didn’t care for country music. But strangely enough, as a kid I used to hear it…

842.t: Audiences, rock and roll and Elvis
842.s: Fraternity crowds loved the music, rock and roll came after college, and a view on Elvis as watershed.
842.q: Not in those days. They loved the stuff. And that’s I think the sad part of the world for me today is that the audience is going away. It was so much fun. I mean you’d go in and you’d have just throngs of people. You know on a nice spring evening you’d wind up on some terrace you know and half the…

759.t: Rock and roll backbeats and Charlie Watts
759.s: Monk asks about Butch's early dislike of rock and roll beats; Butch spells out the patterns and praises classic simple grooves.
759.q: Or, if you really felt adventurous, it was boom-whack-boom-boom-whack-whack. Or boom-whack-whack-boom-whack-boom-whack, which, to his credit, Charlie Watts still plays, to this day.

554.t: Rock and roll gigs he could not do
554.s: He quit a band that became eighty percent rock and roll because he would not memorize record riffs.
554.q: I’ve had to play a few gigs before. I was playing with one group that at first it was only ten percent rock & roll, then it came to be eighty percent rock & roll so I didn’t stay with the band but you had to play certain things like they had these disco things or else the saxophone player had to…

349.t: Rock and roll, brushes, and playing rock tunes with his drummer
349.s: He finds rock disorganized, tells of a drummer scorning brushes, and describes playing blues/rock with a versatile drummer.
349.q: Well I’ll tell you about rock & roll. I can’t say I have the greatest respect for it because a lot of times it’s very disorganized, the music that is.

443.t: Rock Around the Clock, the rock takeover and Princeton
443.s: He recalls jazz bands vanishing from Princeton by 1960 and the Rock Around the Clock riot. He discusses bebop losing the dancing public and rock's roots in swing and R&B.
443.q: Well within two years after graduating, by 1960 I was invited back to play at one of the clubs for one of the football weekends. And when I was there as late as 1958 there might have been, on a party weekend, on a football weekend, eight jazz bands from New York at Princeton, cause Princeton is 60…

716.t: Rock Around the Clock and rock and roll's roots
716.s: They argue whether the song swings; he says it predates swing and traces rock and roll to 1921 blues.
716.q: Well the feel of it is about screwing to the clock. I mean that’s what the song is about. That’s what rock & roll actually means.

360.t: Rock and roll and playing what audiences wanted
360.s: Rock and roll made no impression on him; he did play rhythm and blues when audiences asked.
360.q: No it didn’t make an impression on me at all. Because I’m just jazz oriented. I liked it, but I only can take so much of it and then I’m going to go back to my comfort zone.

217.t: Rock and roll and good versus bad music
217.s: Rock and roll had no effect on him; there are only good and bad kinds of music.
217.q: Well you don’t make the same kind of money that rock & rollers made. But I’ve never paid any attention to it, because I never listened to it, and it doesn’t interest me. Simple as that.

671.t: Rock and roll, Bull Moose Jackson, Coltrane and walking the bar
671.s: Rock and roll affected work; he played in Bull Moose Jackson's band with Coltrane, and discusses bar-walking players including Paul Weaver's.
671.ch: Back in Ohio, Philadelphia and the 1950s
671.q: Oh it affected it quite a bit, yeah. As a matter of fact I never have — I remember when it first started I was in Philadelphia and I worked with Bull Moose Jackson, and he had a big band. And they had a Rock band there. One answer is probably they were loud. They were good and loud. As a matter of…

122.t: Bebop, Dixieland and doo wop: changing tastes and the money
122.s: Musical controversies, his fascination with bebop, and how young listeners' disposable income shifted work to doo wop.
122.ch: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
122.q: So there is always a controversy. I mean even if you read history in New Orleans, how there seemed to be controversies. You have the different schools. As I guess each age has its musical culture, musical taste, their fad, or whatever you want to call it. So I’m speaking for myself. I came up in…

368.t: A double bill with Bill Haley and the Comets
368.s: In Philadelphia he found himself opening for Bill Haley and the Comets.
368.ch: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
368.q: Yeah, that was a strange situation. I played; it was at a club, famous club in Philadelphia. In fact, the owner at that time was married to Barbara Walters. And, usually we were booked with other jazz groups that I was familiar with, one time I played opposite Oscar’s group. This time I had another…

116.t: Modes, the 1964 turning point and the Beatles
116.s: He explains learning modal playing, 1964 civil rights law and the Beatles' effect on jazz audiences.
116.q: That was even earlier. Because when Trane – Trane was already dead by ’68. Just listening at some of the things that he was doing, and the thing that Miles was implementing in terms of modes. But it mostly the stuff that Trane was doing with McCoy [Tyner], trying to figure that out. It was…

134.t: Navarro, McGhee and Diz; why the music declined
134.s: Freeman says the bebop figures faded in the early 1950s and singers and rock and roll came in.
134.ch: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
134.q: . . . yeah, Howard McGhee – all those guys were such a big part of the Chicago scene, because they were all coming to Chicago all the time. They almost all of them dissipated around the same time.

680.t: The idea of combining rock and jazz
680.s: Leaving Getz, Burton reasons he must reach his own generation, citing his love of the Beatles and Dylan and taking the Getz family to Shea Stadium.
680.ch: George Wein and forming the quartet
680.q: I left Stan and wanted to start a new band. My idea was to somehow combine rock music with jazz. I got that idea in sort of a calculated business way, which is... Normally you don’t get great ideas that way. But I was trying to be very practical, and I said: Ok, all my audiences up to now have been…

16.t: Rock and roll in the 1960s and Miss Teen USA
16.s: He says rock initially seemed inconsequential, recalls learning boogie-woogie, and describes the Miss Teen USA work.
16.q: Some were and some did. Some affected me musically and some did affect my livelihood. I will have to confess that having been through the heyday of the birth of jazz quote unquote as we know it today, having worked on 52nd Street, having seen first hand the Gillespies and the Charlie Parkers and…

165.t: Jazz and rhythm-and-blues as one music
165.s: He argues jazz and R&B share one source in the spirituals and that rock came from would-be jazz players.
165.q: Very close. One evolved out of the other. Jazz was nothing but a more sophisticated rhythm-and-blues. It’s like the city mouse and the country mouse. The country mouse comes to visit the city mouse, and he lives in a penthouse rather than on a farm. Rhythm-and-blues is like the country version of…

373.t: Rock and roll and the shrinking jazz audience
373.s: He describes the loss of young jazz fans, Teddy Wilson's encouragement and the garage-band generation.
373.ch: Second day: New Yorker, Dylan and comedians
373.q: My take was the diminishment of the audience for jazz, because until then, I think it’s fair to say generalizingly that even though jazz was never a popular music – I mean Benny Goodman was popular for a time because he played dances that got radio appearances, etc. – but there was always a nucleus…

27.t: Jazz dying in 1954 as rock and roll arrives
27.s: Harry Curtis led a band of a few gigs around 1954, when jazz work was disappearing.
27.ch: Rhythm and blues, the Howard Theatre and later years
27.q: Yeah, he was in there with John. He got a band himself around '54. We just gigged. That was about three gigs. Doin' pretty good. The music was dying then. That's when it was goin' down, round about '54. Rock-and-Roll was comin' in like Faust. Rock-and-Roll and Rhythm-and-Blues. People wasn't carin'…

382.t: Rhythm and blues and the crisis in popular music before her retirement
382.s: Back from Britain she found the singers doing rhythm and blues; she felt there was no place for her style.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: Yeah. What I was saying is when I came back off that tour of Great Britain I was trying like mad to get a record because I didn't have a contract with any recording company. I was just, if anything came up and somebody wanted to make a record, you know, I was there. But I had material I wanted to…

120.t: Rock takes over the Canadian club
120.s: Jazz rooms turn to rock; the Colonial Inn, where his band had packed the place, brings in flashing lights and go-go girls.
120.ch: Looking back and the lean years
120.q: Finally, I just had to move back. And, so, this is what I'm talking about - when anyone asks you - how did you survive -- those years and then, of course, you know Rock was big and coming in strong as hell, you know, and it was just putting a lot of guys-- a lot of jazz places in America were…

385.t: Rock and roll pushes jazz aside
385.s: Rock and roll took over from rhythm and blues, and the audience supported it while jazz fans did not.
385.ch: Metronome, Billie Holiday, Cleveland and Atlantic
385.q: - Yeah, we were -- call rhythm and blues, you know, and they started puttin' this hard drum things and these hard beats and they named it rock and roll, and that kind of started takin' over, and just put the jazz musician way back.

235.t: Rock and roll takes over the clubs
235.s: With rock and roll the owners wanted something new and club dates were all that was left.
235.ch: After the Paradise: club dates and Virginia
235.q: : Club dates. Yeah, that was all that was left because rock and roll came in and so the people went for that, you know, owners and what not, you know, "This is new; this is new." So what are you going to do? You can't fight city hall. So I went into that because you know that every week you're…

387.t: Rock, guitars and the star system
387.s: Early rock sparked 'I can do that' attitudes and a star system.
387.q: I remember in the forties, and the thirties, this sort of thing going on, but it wasn't so all encompassing as it is now.

75.t: Bebop not danceable; Latin and Rock-and-Roll
75.s: Bebop was not danceable, so Latin and Rock-and-Roll came into vogue.
75.q: When you take... The thing is, the advent of Rock-and-Roll came to be during the era when Bebop and all those fast rhythms were not danceable. It's not like the Big Band Era, where you can dance to it. You'd grab a girl, and you would say, 'Well, let me get into the act.' Well, now, sitting down…
